front_blocks.md: Define **moment**.

back_blocks.md: The **moment** of a force is the **turning effect** produced when a force is exerted on an object, causing rotation about a **pivot**.

cards.back_md: The **moment** of a force is the **turning effect** produced when a force is exerted on an object, causing rotation about a **pivot**.

front_blocks.md: Define **pivot**.

back_blocks.md: A **pivot** is the fixed point about which an object can rotate.

cards.back_md: A **pivot** is the fixed point about which an object can rotate.

front_blocks.md: State the equation for the moment of a force, including the units of each quantity.

back_blocks.md: $M = F \times d$
Where:

- *M* = moment in newton metres (N m)
- *F* = force in newtons (N)
- *d* = perpendicular distance from the pivot in metres (m)

front_blocks.md: Why does increasing the distance a force is applied from a pivot decrease the force needed to produce the same moment?

back_blocks.md: Since moment = force × distance, a fixed moment can be produced by a **smaller force** if the **distance** from the pivot is **increased** — this is why a door is easier to push open at the handle (far from the hinge) than close to the hinge.

front_blocks.md: On a horizontal beam, only forces that are **______** to the distance from the pivot will cause a moment.

back_blocks.md: On a horizontal beam, only forces that are **perpendicular** to the distance from the pivot will cause a moment.

cards.front_md: On a horizontal beam, only forces that are **______** to the distance from the pivot will cause a moment.
cards.back_md: On a horizontal beam, only forces that are **perpendicular** to the distance from the pivot will cause a moment.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The moment of a force can only be measured in newton metres (N m).

back_blocks.md: **False.**

The moment can also be measured in **newton centimetres (N cm)** if the distance is measured in centimetres; in an IGCSE exam, distances should be converted to **metres** unless a specific unit is requested.

front_blocks.md: Give two examples of everyday situations where the moment of a force causes rotation.

back_blocks.md: Any two from: turning the handle of a **spanner**, opening/closing a **door**, using a **screwdriver**, turning a **tap**, lifting a **wheelbarrow**, using **scissors**, a child on a **see-saw**, or a **crane** moving building supplies.

front_blocks.md: Define the **principle of moments**.

back_blocks.md: If an object is **balanced**, the total **clockwise moment** about a pivot equals the total **anticlockwise moment** about that pivot.

cards.back_md: If an object is **balanced**, the total **clockwise moment** about a pivot equals the total **anticlockwise moment** about that pivot.

front_blocks.md: A parent weighing 690 N sits 0.3 m from the pivot of a see-saw. A child weighing 140 N sits on the opposite side. Calculate the distance the child must sit from the pivot for the see-saw to balance.

back_blocks.md: Anticlockwise moment (parent) = 690 × 0.3 = 207 N m
For balance: clockwise moment (child) = anticlockwise moment
140 × *d*<sub>child</sub> = 207

cards.front_md: A parent weighing 690 N sits 0.3 m from the pivot of a see-saw. A child weighing 140 N sits on the opposite side. Calculate the distance the child must sit from the pivot for the see-saw to balance.
cards.back_md:
Anticlockwise moment (parent) = 690 × 0.3 = 207 N m

For balance: clockwise moment (child) = anticlockwise moment

140 × *d*<sub>child</sub> = 207

*d*<sub>child</sub> = $\frac{207}{140}$ = **1.5 m** (2 s.f.)

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A horizontal force applied to a horizontal beam will produce a moment about the pivot.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Only forces **perpendicular** to the distance from the pivot produce a moment; on a horizontal beam, this means only forces directed **upwards or downwards** cause a moment.

front_blocks.md: Define a **light beam** (as used in moments problems).

back_blocks.md: A **light beam** is one that can be treated as having **no mass**, so any supports need only balance the weight of objects placed on it.

front_blocks.md: The supports of a beam must exert **______** forces that balance the downward-acting weight of any object placed on the beam.

back_blocks.md: The supports of a beam must exert **upward** forces that balance the downward-acting weight of any object placed on the beam.

cards.front_md: The supports of a beam must exert **______** forces that balance the downward-acting weight of any object placed on the beam.
cards.back_md: The supports of a beam must exert **upward** forces that balance the downward-acting weight of any object placed on the beam.

front_blocks.md: A mass is moved from the left-hand side towards the right-hand side of a beam supported at both ends. What happens to the supporting forces *F*<sub>1</sub> (left) and *F*<sub>2</sub> (right)?

back_blocks.md: *F*<sub>1</sub> (left) **decreases** and *F*<sub>2</sub> (right) **increases** as the mass moves towards the right-hand support.

cards.front_md: A mass is moved from the left-hand side towards the right-hand side of a beam supported at both ends. What happens to the supporting forces *F*<sub>1</sub> (left) and *F*<sub>2</sub> (right)?
cards.back_md: *F*<sub>1</sub> (left) **decreases** and *F*<sub>2</sub> (right) **increases** as the mass moves towards the right-hand support.

front_blocks.md: A beam is supported at both ends with an object placed on it. What happens if the right-hand support is removed?

back_blocks.md: The force at the right-hand support becomes **zero**, so it can no longer supply the **anticlockwise moment** needed to balance the object's weight — the beam rotates in the **clockwise** direction about the left-hand support.

front_blocks.md: Define **centre of gravity**.

back_blocks.md: The **centre of gravity** of an object is the point through which the **weight** of the object acts.

cards.back_md: The **centre of gravity** of an object is the point through which the **weight** of the object acts.

front_blocks.md: Where is the centre of gravity located for a symmetrical object of uniform density? Give an example.

back_blocks.md: It is located at the **point of symmetry** — for example, the centre of gravity of a **sphere** is at its centre.

cards.front_md: Where is the centre of gravity located for a symmetrical object of uniform density? Give an example.

front_blocks.md: Define a **plumb line**.

back_blocks.md: A **plumb line** is a weighted thread that hangs vertically; it is used to mark a vertical reference line down from a suspension point when locating an object's centre of mass.

cards.back_md: A **plumb line** is a weighted thread that hangs vertically; it is used to mark a vertical reference line down from a suspension point when locating an object's centre of mass.

front_blocks.md: To find the centre of mass of an irregular lamina, it is suspended from a pivot and a plumb line is used to draw a vertical line; this is repeated from two more suspension points, and the centre of mass lies where the three lines **______**.

back_blocks.md: To find the centre of mass of an irregular lamina, it is suspended from a pivot and a plumb line is used to draw a vertical line; this is repeated from two more suspension points, and the centre of mass lies where the three lines **cross**.

cards.front_md: To find the centre of mass of an irregular lamina, it is suspended from a pivot and a plumb line is used to draw a vertical line; this is repeated from two more suspension points, and the centre of mass lies where the three lines **______**.
cards.back_md: To find the centre of mass of an irregular lamina, it is suspended from a pivot and a plumb line is used to draw a vertical line; this is repeated from two more suspension points, and the centre of mass lies where the three lines **cross**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The centre of mass of an irregular lamina can be located using just one suspension point.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

The lamina must be suspended from **at least three different points**, with a plumb line drawn each time; the centre of mass is where the three lines **intersect** — a single point only shows the centre of mass lies somewhere along that one line.
